issue_context.title: Method overload resolution: [NullString]::Value doesn't guide toward picking a [string]-based overload
issue_context.body:
### Prerequisites

- [X] Write a descriptive title.
- [X] Make sure you are able to repro it on the [latest released version](https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/releases)
- [X] Search the existing issues.
- [X] Refer to the [FAQ](https://github.com/PowerShell/PowerShell/blob/master/docs/FAQ.md).
- [X] Refer to [Differences between Windows PowerShell 5.1 and PowerShell](https://docs.microsoft.com/powershell/scripting/whats-new/differences-from-windows-powershell).

### Steps to reproduce

` [NullString]::Value` was specifically introduced to pass a true `$null` value to `string`-typed method parameters.
Yet, during method overload resolution, it doesn't reliably select a `[string]`-based overload:

```powershell
class Foo {
  [string] Test([bool] $bar) { return 'bool'}
  [string] Test([string] $bar) { return 'string' }
}

# *Should* select the `[string]` overload, but doesn't.
[Foo]::new().Test([NullString]::Value)
# OK, with cast:
[Foo]::new().Test([string] [NullString]::Value)
```


### Expected behavior

```console
string
string
```


### Actual behavior

```console
bool
string
```


### Error details

_No response_

### Environment data

```powershell
PowerShell Core 7.3.0-preview.7
```


### Visuals

_No response_
comments:
Can I get some background on why `NullString` was introduced? Shouldn't `[string] $null` work already, or was it broken and deemed a breaking change to fix?

It looks like the `[NullString]::Value` prefers implicit conversion of null to false over implicit conversion to string. Don't quite remember C#'s implicit conversion rules to say how easy of a fix it would be.

Can you play around with other overload sets? What if you add an explicit overload for `[NullString]`? Or something that it does not covert to, e.g. some other struct, but skip the bool one?

`[string] $null` passes the empty string, not null: `'' -eq [string] $null` is `$true`.
This behavior also applies when passing `$null` to .NET methods, which - prior to the introduction of `[NullString]::Value` - made it impossible to pass true `null` to `string` parameters of .NET APIs.

> What if you add an explicit overload for `[NullString]`?

The above implies that `[NullString]` isn't meant to be used as an actual type; its `::Value` property merely serves to indicate that it should be _translated to `null`_ in string contexts.

Because `[NullString]::Value` is a singleton of a [distinct type](https://docs.microsoft.com/en-US/dotnet/api/System.Management.Automation.Language.NullString), it should be easy to distinguish it from `$null` during overload resolution.

review_comments: Why replace LINQ `All` with a `foreach`? The former looks way clearer to me, I don't need to analyse what the loop does, the algorithm is clearly stated.

> Why replace LINQ `All` with a `foreach`? The former looks way clearer to me, I don't need to analyse what the loop does, the algorithm is clearly stated.

It's an abstraction that isn't free unfortunately. In most places it's fine, but performance sensitive code should avoid it when possible.

Do you have some performance measurements to show the difference? Or, more generally, does PowerShell have performance regression tests in CI?

Back at university I wrote a constraint solver that was pretty much just couple dozen expression-bodied functions immediately returning a LINQ expression. So every single line of LINQ was in hot path. I benched it against unrolled for loops and saw no statistically significant difference. And that was 5 years ago, I would imagine compiler/runtime get even better in optimizing abstractions to make them zero cost.

I could imagine this logic being required in the future for different types, so hardcoding it here in the ternary does not look maintainable to me. How about making `NullString` implement something like `interface ITypeOverloadOverride { Type TypeForOverloadResolution`? Then you could replace this ternary with a generic `obj is ITypeOverloadOverride overridden ? overridden?.TypeForOverloadResolution : obj?.GetType();`

> I could imagine this logic being required in the future for different types, so hardcoding it here in the ternary does not look maintainable to me. How about making `NullString` implement something like `interface ITypeOverloadOverride { Type TypeForOverloadResolution`? Then you could replace this ternary with a generic `obj is ITypeOverloadOverride overridden ? overridden?.TypeForOverloadResolution : obj?.GetType();`

`NullString` is a bit of a special case because it's the only type PowerShell tries to pretend as if it's a valuetype. I don't think it's likely we'll have to add another. Maybe would be a good issue to open but out of scope of this PR imo

I'd rather keep the old descriptive name `argAsArray` the new `array` leaves no clue about what the variable holds, its like a `String string` or `int i` - fine in some context, don't see a point in changing it here.
The `is` expression makes the variable quite descriptive, as in "arg is an array".

I think I know C# pretty well but never considered it from performance side. In C++, this function would be almost guaranteed to be inlined and the `if` discarded or made unconditional. Is C#'s optimizer really not capable of it? Do you have some optimization guidelines I could read, e.g. when to use `[AggressivelyInline]` I saw in some `WriteToConsole` overloads?
This seems to be a micro-optimization that we should avoid, as I don't think the difference is measurable.
Same as above: LINQ is more readable
